dataset.description: Phase 7 golden evaluation dataset for the Nexora Commerce permission-aware enterprise RAG system. Ground truth only: it is never written to by an evaluation run. Authorization expectations are NOT restated here; the runner derives them from the Phase 4 permission engine and the Phase 2 document catalog. 'expected_sources' names the authorized documents a correct answer must be grounded in; 'forbidden_sources' names the specific documents this case is probing, and the runner additionally checks the complete derived deny-list for the identity. Source-reviewed remediation v1.2; alternative-source answers are permitted with explicit attribution.

This document covers the onboarding of GreenCart Organics Pvt. Ltd. (S003), a subscription-first organic grocery business, and records the closure position handed to the account team. GreenCart was the first perishable-category seller onboarded on the platform, so several standard onboarding assumptions had to be varied.
2. What Made This Onboarding Different
Three characteristics separated GreenCart from previous onboardings.
Perishable goods. A missed delivery slot is a write-off, not a reschedule. Standard dispatch SLA definitions,
which assume a failed delivery can be retried the next day, do not hold. Fulfilment requirements were therefore expressed against delivery slots rather than against dispatch windows.
Subscription ordering. GreenCart's customers buy a recurring weekly basket. Orders arrive in predictable batches tied to slot cut-offs rather than being distributed through the day. Capacity planning is concentrated rather than smooth, and a failure at a slot cut-off affects an entire cohort at once.
Connector-based integration. GreenCart runs its storefront on Shopify and did not have the engineering capacity to build a direct integration. This document records the onboarding of StrideOne Footwear Pvt. Ltd. (S004) and the delivery of its dropship integration. StrideOne holds no inventory of its own; orders are routed to third-party logistics partners who hold brand stock. 2. The Dropship Model
In a conventional marketplace integration the seller owns stock, knows where it is, and dispatches it.
StrideOne owns none of these things.
 Stock is held by four third-party logistics partners, each with its own systems and its own view of availability.

 Returns are received by the partner, so return reason data flows back through the partner rather than from StrideOne.

1. Scope of These Notes
These notes describe how GreenCart Organics (S003) is technically integrated with the platform, and record the behaviour of the integration during the two production incidents on this account in 2026. They are written for engineers who need to reason about where a fault lies when GreenCart reports a problem.
The central point is that GreenCart's integration has three layers, and most confusion on this account comes from attributing a fault to the wrong one.
Layer
Owned by
Typical failure signature

GreenCart

Connector bridge
Platform, shared operation

Nexora platform services
Platform

duplication
2. Order Intake Path
An order placed on the marketplace is delivered to the connector by webhook. The connector translates it into a Shopify order object, applies the delivery slot as a line-item property, and acknowledges. GreenCart's dark store systems read from Shopify.
Important characteristics:
 Delivery is at-least-once. The connector deduplicates on the platform order identifier before creating a Shopify order.
 Slot metadata travels as a line-item property, not as an order-level field.
This was a Shopify modelling constraint and is the reason the pilot found an amendment defect in August
2025.
 Acknowledgement is fast and processing is asynchronous, so a slow Shopify
API does not cause webhook retries at the platform end.
3. Inventory Path
Stock is maintained per dark store. The connector publishes availability at slot granularity: a SKU can be available for tomorrow's morning slot and unavailable for tonight's, because stock is allocated against slot capacity rather than against a single pool.

5.1 Scenario SC-004 - Tax Invoice Mismatch (February 2026)
After an HSN revision, newly listed decorative lighting SKUs were not mapped to the 12 percent slab and defaulted to 18 percent. 1,240 invoices were issued at the wrong rate, producing a reconciliation mismatch of
INR 2,17,600. The mapping was corrected, credit notes were re-issued and a validation check was added to the listing workflow. The commercial decision and its rationale are recorded in the account decision record.
5.2 Scenario SC-001 - Settlement Shortfall (March 2026)
The settlement batch covering 5 to 9 March 2026 was short by INR 4,82,000. Engineering traced this to a deduplication key defect in the settlement ledger introduced during a schema migration, which double-deducted 1,914 reversal entries. The shortfall was credited on 14 March 2026. This is the highest-severity financial event on the account and remains the reference case for the reconciliation hardening project.
5.3 Scenario SC-010 - Checkout Regression (August 2026)
A platform-wide checkout release defect caused roughly 7 percent of cart-to-payment transitions to fail.
Aurelia was not the cause and was one of several affected sellers, but its festive pre-season traffic made the impact visible on the account. The release was rolled back within 34 minutes.

financial queries outnumber technical ones. Ritika Bansal raises tickets with precise order-level evidence attached, which shortens triage considerably. Rahul Sharma is the named support owner and handles the majority of the account's escalations.
 Settlement and payout queries: approximately 45 percent of ticket volume.
 Invoicing and tax queries: approximately 20 percent.
 Order and checkout failures: approximately 20 percent.
 Catalogue and listing questions: approximately 15 percent.
7. Current Watch Items
1. Settlement reconciliation hardening. The project opened after SC-001
is still in progress; automated variance detection is live but the seller-facing variance statement is pending.
2. Festive readiness. The account team must confirm inventory buffers and support cover before the late-September peak.
3. Tax mapping validation. The control added after SC-004 should be verified once the next HSN revision is published.

That was enough to confirm the seller was right and that this was not a reconciliation misunderstanding. I did not attempt further diagnosis, because duplicated ledger entries are a platform data problem rather than a configuration problem.
Escalation
Escalated to Engineering at 11:20 IST on 12 March, within the P1 escalation window defined in the Seller
Escalation Policy (POL-BIZ-004). Vikram Singh picked it up and opened incident INC-2026-0312.
I also flagged the ticket to Aditya Verma at 11:25 IST, because Aurelia's finance team reconciles every cycle and a two-day payout delay on a Gold account needed an account-manager conversation rather than a support update.

Root Cause as Reported Back to Support
Engineering found that the deduplication key used by the settlement ledger no longer included the order identifier for reversal entries. The key was changed during the v1.8 to v1.9 schema migration. When the batch was reprocessed after a transient job failure, the ledger treated each reversal as a new entry rather than as an existing one, so every reversal was deducted a second time.
Full technical detail is in INC-2026-0312.
Resolution
The deduplication key was corrected to include order identifier plus entry type. The affected batch was reprocessed, Operations verified the corrected payout against the Payment Recovery Runbook
(OPS-RB-004), and INR 4,82,000 was credited on 14 March 2026. The applicable rule is the platform's accountability for the accuracy of a computed settlement under the Payment and Settlement Policy
(POL-FIN-002).

Project status
5.1 Scenario SC-004 - Tax Invoice Mismatch (February 2026)
After an HSN revision, newly listed decorative lighting SKUs were not mapped to the 12 percent slab and defaulted to 18 percent. 1,240 invoices were issued at the wrong rate, producing a reconciliation mismatch of
INR 2,17,600. The mapping was corrected, credit notes were re-issued and a validation check was added to the listing workflow. The commercial decision and its rationale are recorded in the account decision record.
5.2 Scenario SC-001 - Settlement Shortfall (March 2026)
The settlement batch covering 5 to 9 March 2026 was short by INR 4,82,000. Engineering traced this to a deduplication key defect in the settlement ledger introduced during a schema migration, which double-deducted 1,914 reversal entries. The shortfall was credited on 14 March 2026. This is the highest-severity financial event on the account and remains the reference case for the reconciliation hardening project.
5.3 Scenario SC-010 - Checkout Regression (August 2026)
A platform-wide checkout release defect caused roughly 7 percent of cart-to-payment transitions to fail.
Aurelia was not the cause and was one of several affected sellers, but its festive pre-season traffic made the impact visible on the account. The release was rolled back within 34 minutes.
6. Support Profile
Aurelia raises a moderate number of tickets, typically 8 to 14 per quarter, and the distribution is unusual:
financial queries outnumber technical ones. Ritika Bansal raises tickets with precise order-level evidence attached, which shortens triage considerably. Rahul Sharma is the named support owner and handles the majority of the account's escalations.
 Settlement and payout queries: approximately 45 percent of ticket volume.
 Invoicing and tax queries: approximately 20 percent.
 Order and checkout failures: approximately 20 percent.
 Catalogue and listing questions: approximately 15 percent.
7. Current Watch Items
1. Settlement reconciliation hardening. The project opened after SC-001
is still in progress; automated variance detection is live but the seller-facing variance statement is pending.
2. Festive readiness. The account team must confirm inventory buffers and support cover before the late-September peak.
3. Tax mapping validation. The control added after SC-004 should be verified once the next HSN revision is published.

2. Business Profile
Aurelia Home Decor designs and manufactures its own range of home furnishings. Unlike a reseller, Aurelia controls its entire catalogue, which means listing quality is consistently high and attribute disputes are rare.
The trade-off is that production lead times are long: a stock-out on a handwoven product line can take six to eight weeks to recover, so Aurelia manages inventory conservatively and reacts strongly to any platform issue that causes phantom stock or cancelled orders.
Revenue is heavily seasonal. Roughly 38 percent of annual gross merchandise value is transacted between late September and early January, around the festive and wedding seasons. A second, smaller peak occurs in March. The account team plans catalogue campaigns, inventory buffers and support readiness around these two windows.
Aurelia's commercial sensitivity is concentrated in two areas: settlement accuracy and tax correctness.
The finance team at Aurelia reconciles every payout line against its own order export and raises a query whenever the variance exceeds one percent. This is why two of the three scenarios recorded against this account in 2026 are financial rather than technical in origin.

results.question: What was the root cause of the BluePeak Electronics inventory synchronisation drift on 19 May 2026?
results.answer:
The drift was caused by two independent faults: the nightly batch scheduler used a fixed UTC offset instead of the Asia/Kolkata timezone, causing it to process the previous night’s stock file and introduce about 24 hours of staleness, and a legacy SKU‑mapping table retained as a silent fallback resolved rows against outdated mappings, adding roughly two more hours of apparent staleness and misdirected inventory.

7. Investigation
7.1 The Proximate Cause
Order placement calls the inventory lookup service synchronously. Under normal load that call returns in about 40 ms. Under flash-sale load it slowed to 600-900 ms, because the lookup fans out across a much larger set of SKUs than a typical order.
Each in-flight placement holds a connection from a fixed pool of 120 for the duration of that call. At 9x baseline traffic with a 15x slower dependency, demand for connections exceeded 120 within about four minutes. Once the pool was full, new requests queued with no acquisition timeout and eventually returned
503.
7.2 The Amplification
The failure would have been self-limiting if clients had backed off. They did not.
BluePeak's client retried timed-out placements without limit and without backoff. Every 503 produced another request. Measured inbound volume at 20:18 was approximately 3.4 times the volume implied by actual buyer activity, so roughly 70 percent of the traffic at peak was retries of already-failed requests.
This is why no static capacity figure would have been sufficient. An unbounded retry loop expands to consume whatever capacity exists.
7.3 The Missing Control
The inventory lookup had no circuit breaker. A slow dependency should eventually be bypassed or failed fast, so that callers release their connections. Instead, every caller waited the full timeout, and the timeout on that path was 10 seconds.
A 10-second timeout with a 120-connection pool caps throughput at 12 requests per second once the dependency is slow, regardless of how much capacity the service otherwise has.
8. Root Cause
The order service connection pool was exhausted because synchronous inventory lookups slowed under flash-sale load and were not protected by a circuit breaker or an acquisition timeout, while an unbounded client retry policy amplified inbound traffic to roughly 3.4 times genuine demand. The combination converted a capacity pressure into a 40-minute cascading failure.
9. Contributing Factors

7. Investigation
7.1 The Scheduler Fault
The batch selects a stock window relative to the run time. The window calculation used a fixed UTC offset constant rather than resolving Asia/Kolkata.
BluePeak delivers its stock file at approximately 23:00 IST. The job runs at 02:00 IST. Under correct behaviour the job selects the window ending at the most recent file delivery. Under the fixed-offset calculation the window boundary fell 5 hours 30 minutes earlier, before the file was delivered, so the job selected the previous night's file.
This alone produced roughly 24 hours of staleness.
7.2 The Mapping Fault
The March 2026 catalogue restructure introduced new catalogue identifiers. A migration mapped old seller
SKUs to new identifiers and wrote a new mapping table. The legacy table was retained as a fallback for rows that failed to resolve against the new table, and the fallback was never removed.
Rows failing to resolve against the current mapping silently resolved against the legacy table. Where the legacy mapping pointed at a catalogue identifier that had since been reassigned, stock was published against the wrong SKU. Where the legacy mapping pointed at an identifier that no longer existed, the row was dropped without report.
This explains the uneven distribution and the missing SKUs, and added up to a further two hours of apparent staleness where stock landed on the wrong identifier.
7.3 Why Neither Alone Was Sufficient
The freshness requirement is six hours. The scheduler fault alone produced about 24 hours of staleness,
which would have breached the requirement had anything been measuring it. Nothing was. The mapping fault alone produced incorrect rather than stale data, which would have surfaced as individual SKU
complaints rather than as a systemic pattern.
Together they produced a large, visible, systemic failure that the seller detected within days. Paradoxically,
the combination is what made the problem detectable at all.
8. Root Cause
The nightly stock batch published stale and partially misdirected inventory because the scheduler computed its window using a fixed UTC offset rather than the Asia/Kolkata timezone, causing it to process the previous

night's file, and because a legacy SKU mapping table retained as a silent fallback resolved rows that should have been rejected.
9. Contributing Factors
1. No freshness metric. The pipeline measured completion, not currency.
2. A silent fallback. The legacy mapping made a failure look like a success. A strict rejection would have surfaced the problem in March.
3. Implicit timezone handling. The scheduler relied on a constant rather than an explicit timezone, a pattern not specific to this job.
4. Migration cleanup incomplete. The March restructure left a fallback in place with no removal date or owner.
5. Requirement not enforced. The six-hour freshness requirement existed in the integration specification but had no corresponding control.
10. Mitigation
The effective mitigation was the seller disabling affected listings at 10:35 on 19 May, which stopped new oversells within about 20 minutes. This was the seller's decision, taken on a call with Support, and it was the right one: continuing to trade on unreliable availability would have compounded the harm for the 24 hours needed to correct the pipeline.
No platform-side mitigation was available that would have been faster. The correct stock position could not be published until the pipeline was fixed.

**Root Cause**

The inventory‑synchronisation drift for BluePeak Electronics on 19 May 2026 was caused by **two independent faults that together produced stale and partially misdirected inventory data**:

1. **Scheduler fault** – The nightly stock batch scheduler applied a fixed UTC offset instead of the correct Asia/Kolkata timezone. This caused the job to select the previous night’s stock file, introducing roughly 24 hours of staleness.

2. **Mapping fault** – A legacy SKU‑mapping table, left over from the March 2026 catalogue restructure, was still used as a silent fallback. Rows that should have been rejected were resolved against this outdated table, resulting in stock being published against wrong SKUs or being dropped entirely, adding up to about 2 additional hours of apparent staleness.

Because neither issue alone would have breached the six‑hour freshness requirement, the combination created a large, systemic failure that manifested as the drift detected on 19 May.

7.1 The Proximate Cause
Order placement calls the inventory lookup service synchronously. Under normal load that call returns in about 40 ms. Under flash-sale load it slowed to 600-900 ms, because the lookup fans out across a much larger set of SKUs than a typical order.
Each in-flight placement holds a connection from a fixed pool of 120 for the duration of that call. At 9x baseline traffic with a 15x slower dependency, demand for connections exceeded 120 within about four minutes. 503.
7.2 The Amplification
The failure would have been self-limiting if clients had backed off. They did not.
BluePeak's client retried timed-out placements without limit and without backoff. Every 503 produced another request. Measured inbound volume at 20:18 was approximately 3.4 times the volume implied by actual buyer activity, so roughly 70 percent of the traffic at peak was retries of already-failed requests.
This is why no static capacity figure would have been sufficient. An unbounded retry loop expands to consume whatever capacity exists.
7.3 The Missing Control
The inventory lookup had no circuit breaker. A slow dependency should eventually be bypassed or failed fast, so that callers release their connections. Instead, every caller waited the full timeout, and the timeout on that path was 10 seconds.
A 10-second timeout with a 120-connection pool caps throughput at 12 requests per second once the dependency is slow, regardless of how much capacity the service otherwise has.

The order service connection pool was exhausted because synchronous inventory lookups slowed under flash-sale load and were not protected by a circuit breaker or an acquisition timeout, while an unbounded client retry policy amplified inbound traffic to roughly 3.4 times genuine demand. The combination converted a capacity pressure into a 40-minute cascading failure.

7. Investigation

The batch selects a stock window relative to the run time. The window calculation used a fixed UTC offset constant rather than resolving Asia/Kolkata.
BluePeak delivers its stock file at approximately 23:00 IST. The job runs at 02:00 IST. Under correct behaviour the job selects the window ending at the most recent file delivery. Under the fixed-offset calculation the window boundary fell 5 hours 30 minutes earlier, before the file was delivered, so the job selected the previous night's file.
This alone produced roughly 24 hours of staleness.
7.2 The Mapping Fault
The March 2026 catalogue restructure introduced new catalogue identifiers. A migration mapped old seller
SKUs to new identifiers and wrote a new mapping table. The legacy table was retained as a fallback for rows that failed to resolve against the new table, and the fallback was never removed.
Rows failing to resolve against the current mapping silently resolved against the legacy table. Where the legacy mapping pointed at a catalogue identifier that had since been reassigned, stock was published against the wrong SKU. Where the legacy mapping pointed at an identifier that no longer existed, the row was dropped without report.
This explains the uneven distribution and the missing SKUs, and added up to a further two hours of apparent staleness where stock landed on the wrong identifier.
7.3 Why Neither Alone Was Sufficient
The freshness requirement is six hours. The scheduler fault alone produced about 24 hours of staleness,
which would have breached the requirement had anything been measuring it. Nothing was. The mapping fault alone produced incorrect rather than stale data, which would have surfaced as individual SKU
complaints rather than as a systemic pattern.
Together they produced a large, visible, systemic failure that the seller detected within days. Paradoxically,
the combination is what made the problem detectable at all.

**Root Cause**

The inventory‑synchronisation drift for BluePeak Electronics on 19 May 2026 was caused by **two independent faults that together produced stale and partially misdirected inventory data**:

1. **Scheduler fault** – The nightly stock batch scheduler applied a fixed UTC offset instead of the correct Asia/Kolkata timezone. This caused the job to select the previous night’s stock file, introducing roughly 24 hours of staleness.

2. **Mapping fault** – A legacy SKU‑mapping table, left over from the March 2026 catalogue restructure, was still used as a silent fallback. Rows that should have been rejected were resolved against this outdated table, resulting in stock being published against wrong SKUs or being dropped entirely, adding up to about 2 additional hours of apparent staleness.

Because neither issue alone would have breached the six‑hour freshness requirement, the combination created a large, systemic failure that manifested as the drift detected on 19 May.

7. Investigation
7.1 The Proximate Cause
Order placement calls the inventory lookup service synchronously. Under normal load that call returns in about 40 ms. Under flash-sale load it slowed to 600-900 ms, because the lookup fans out across a much larger set of SKUs than a typical order.
Each in-flight placement holds a connection from a fixed pool of 120 for the duration of that call. At 9x baseline traffic with a 15x slower dependency, demand for connections exceeded 120 within about four minutes. Once the pool was full, new requests queued with no acquisition timeout and eventually returned
503.
7.2 The Amplification
The failure would have been self-limiting if clients had backed off. They did not.
BluePeak's client retried timed-out placements without limit and without backoff. Every 503 produced another request. Measured inbound volume at 20:18 was approximately 3.4 times the volume implied by actual buyer activity, so roughly 70 percent of the traffic at peak was retries of already-failed requests.
This is why no static capacity figure would have been sufficient. An unbounded retry loop expands to consume whatever capacity exists.
7.3 The Missing Control
The inventory lookup had no circuit breaker. A slow dependency should eventually be bypassed or failed fast, so that callers release their connections. Instead, every caller waited the full timeout, and the timeout on that path was 10 seconds.
A 10-second timeout with a 120-connection pool caps throughput at 12 requests per second once the dependency is slow, regardless of how much capacity the service otherwise has.
8. Root Cause
The order service connection pool was exhausted because synchronous inventory lookups slowed under flash-sale load and were not protected by a circuit breaker or an acquisition timeout, while an unbounded client retry policy amplified inbound traffic to roughly 3.4 times genuine demand. The combination converted a capacity pressure into a 40-minute cascading failure.

7. Investigation
7.1 The Scheduler Fault
The batch selects a stock window relative to the run time. The window calculation used a fixed UTC offset constant rather than resolving Asia/Kolkata.
BluePeak delivers its stock file at approximately 23:00 IST. The job runs at 02:00 IST. Under correct behaviour the job selects the window ending at the most recent file delivery. Under the fixed-offset calculation the window boundary fell 5 hours 30 minutes earlier, before the file was delivered, so the job selected the previous night's file.
This alone produced roughly 24 hours of staleness.
7.2 The Mapping Fault
The March 2026 catalogue restructure introduced new catalogue identifiers. A migration mapped old seller
SKUs to new identifiers and wrote a new mapping table. The legacy table was retained as a fallback for rows that failed to resolve against the new table, and the fallback was never removed.
Rows failing to resolve against the current mapping silently resolved against the legacy table. Where the legacy mapping pointed at a catalogue identifier that had since been reassigned, stock was published against the wrong SKU. Where the legacy mapping pointed at an identifier that no longer existed, the row was dropped without report.
This explains the uneven distribution and the missing SKUs, and added up to a further two hours of apparent staleness where stock landed on the wrong identifier.
7.3 Why Neither Alone Was Sufficient
The freshness requirement is six hours. The scheduler fault alone produced about 24 hours of staleness,
which would have breached the requirement had anything been measuring it. Nothing was. The mapping fault alone produced incorrect rather than stale data, which would have surfaced as individual SKU
complaints rather than as a systemic pattern.
Together they produced a large, visible, systemic failure that the seller detected within days. Paradoxically,
the combination is what made the problem detectable at all.

7. Investigation
7.1 The Proximate Cause
Order placement calls the inventory lookup service synchronously. Under normal load that call returns in about 40 ms. Under flash-sale load it slowed to 600-900 ms, because the lookup fans out across a much larger set of SKUs than a typical order.
Each in-flight placement holds a connection from a fixed pool of 120 for the duration of that call. At 9x baseline traffic with a 15x slower dependency, demand for connections exceeded 120 within about four minutes. Once the pool was full, new requests queued with no acquisition timeout and eventually returned
503.
7.2 The Amplification
The failure would have been self-limiting if clients had backed off. They did not.
BluePeak's client retried timed-out placements without limit and without backoff. Every 503 produced another request. Measured inbound volume at 20:18 was approximately 3.4 times the volume implied by actual buyer activity, so roughly 70 percent of the traffic at peak was retries of already-failed requests.
This is why no static capacity figure would have been sufficient. An unbounded retry loop expands to consume whatever capacity exists.
7.3 The Missing Control
The inventory lookup had no circuit breaker. A slow dependency should eventually be bypassed or failed fast, so that callers release their connections. Instead, every caller waited the full timeout, and the timeout on that path was 10 seconds.
A 10-second timeout with a 120-connection pool caps throughput at 12 requests per second once the dependency is slow, regardless of how much capacity the service otherwise has.
8. Root Cause
The order service connection pool was exhausted because synchronous inventory lookups slowed under flash-sale load and were not protected by a circuit breaker or an acquisition timeout, while an unbounded client retry policy amplified inbound traffic to roughly 3.4 times genuine demand. The combination converted a capacity pressure into a 40-minute cascading failure.

7. Investigation
7.1 The Proximate Cause
Order placement calls the inventory lookup service synchronously. Under normal load that call returns in about 40 ms. Under flash-sale load it slowed to 600-900 ms, because the lookup fans out across a much larger set of SKUs than a typical order.
Each in-flight placement holds a connection from a fixed pool of 120 for the duration of that call. At 9x baseline traffic with a 15x slower dependency, demand for connections exceeded 120 within about four minutes. Once the pool was full, new requests queued with no acquisition timeout and eventually returned
503.
7.2 The Amplification
The failure would have been self-limiting if clients had backed off. They did not.
BluePeak's client retried timed-out placements without limit and without backoff. Every 503 produced another request. Measured inbound volume at 20:18 was approximately 3.4 times the volume implied by actual buyer activity, so roughly 70 percent of the traffic at peak was retries of already-failed requests.
This is why no static capacity figure would have been sufficient. An unbounded retry loop expands to consume whatever capacity exists.
7.3 The Missing Control
The inventory lookup had no circuit breaker. A slow dependency should eventually be bypassed or failed fast, so that callers release their connections. Instead, every caller waited the full timeout, and the timeout on that path was 10 seconds.
A 10-second timeout with a 120-connection pool caps throughput at 12 requests per second once the dependency is slow, regardless of how much capacity the service otherwise has.
8. Root Cause
The order service connection pool was exhausted because synchronous inventory lookups slowed under flash-sale load and were not protected by a circuit breaker or an acquisition timeout, while an unbounded client retry policy amplified inbound traffic to roughly 3.4 times genuine demand. results.question: What was the root cause of the S002 credential exposure and what containment actions were taken?
results.answer:
The exposure was caused by a valid production SFTP credential for seller S002 being embedded in a support diagnostic script and shared externally. This occurred because support lacked central diagnostic tooling, the account used a single credential for both staging and production, rotation was manual and had not occurred for 46 months, and no secret‑scanning existed in the CI pipeline.

Containment actions were to rotate the credential immediately, which broke the seller’s feeds for about 80 minutes, and then to issue separate staging and production credentials, complete a 90‑day access‑log review, enable secret scanning in CI with a full repository sweep, implement IP allow‑listing on the SFTP endpoint, deploy automated 90‑day rotation for service credentials, and introduce central support diagnostic tooling with runtime credential resolution.

A valid production SFTP credential for seller S002 was embedded in a support diagnostic script and shared outside the company. 7.3 Why Rotation Was Not Automatic
Credential rotation for seller service accounts was a manual process requiring a scheduled coordination window with the seller. In practice this meant rotation happened rarely. The exposed credential had been in use unchanged since June 2022, approximately 46 months.
8. Root Cause
A valid production SFTP credential for seller S002 was embedded in a support diagnostic script and shared outside the company. The exposure was possible because Support had no central diagnostic tooling that resolved credentials at runtime, because the account used a single credential for both staging and production directories, because credential rotation was manual and had not occurred in 46 months, and because no secret scanning existed in the CI pipeline to detect credentials in code.
9. Contributing Factors
1. No secret scanning in the CI pipeline or in code review.
2. Shared staging and production credential on this account, so a credential believed to be low-risk was in fact production-scoped.
3. Manual rotation with a coordination burden that discouraged it.
4. No IP allowlisting on the endpoint, so a valid credential from any source address would have authenticated.
5. No central support tooling, forcing engineers to handle raw credentials.
6. No periodic access review of long-lived service credentials.
10. Containment
The containment decision was to rotate immediately rather than to schedule a coordinated rotation with the seller. This deliberately broke the seller's feeds for 80 minutes.

service_response.query: What was the root cause of the S002 credential exposure and what containment actions were taken?
service_response.answer:
The exposure was caused by a valid production SFTP credential for seller S002 being embedded in a support diagnostic script and shared externally. This occurred because support lacked central diagnostic tooling, the account used a single credential for both staging and production, rotation was manual and had not occurred for 46 months, and no secret‑scanning existed in the CI pipeline.

Containment actions were to rotate the credential immediately, which broke the seller’s feeds for about 80 minutes, and then to issue separate staging and production credentials, complete a 90‑day access‑log review, enable secret scanning in CI with a full repository sweep, implement IP allow‑listing on the SFTP endpoint, deploy automated 90‑day rotation for service credentials, and introduce central support diagnostic tooling with runtime credential resolution.

service_response.query: What was the root cause of the S002 credential exposure and what containment actions were taken?
service_response.answer:
The exposure was caused by a valid production SFTP credential for seller S002 being embedded in a support diagnostic script and shared externally. This occurred because support lacked central diagnostic tooling, the account used a single credential for both staging and production, rotation was manual and had not occurred for 46 months, and no secret‑scanning existed in the CI pipeline.

This resulted in 640 orders being refunded twice, over‑refunding a total of INR 1,18,000.

The near-exclusive concentration on S003 was the first thing I checked and the first thing I reported. It was not because the defect was account-specific. It was because GreenCart's refund-on-report category exception means this account generates far more refund events per order than any other seller, so a defect in refund processing surfaces here first.
Escalation
Escalated to Engineering at 17:48 IST. The pattern - exactly two applications of the same refund, within a narrow window, concentrated on the account with the highest refund event volume - pointed at event redelivery rather than at a calculation error, and I said so in the escalation note.
Operations was included because any recovery from a seller settlement needs an operations decision, not a support decision.
Cause
The refund webhook consumer restarted during a deployment at 21:12 on 2 September. The broker redelivered events that had been processed but not acknowledged. The consumer applied refunds without checking an idempotency key, so each redelivered event produced a second refund.
Detail is in INC-2026-0903.
The Recovery Question
This was the substance of the ticket, more than the technical cause.
Operations decided that the excess INR 1,18,000 would be recovered across four settlement cycles rather than in a single deduction, and that no interest or fee would apply. The reasoning was that the seller did not cause the error and a single large debit on a cash-constrained account would have caused real operational harm for no benefit to the platform.
Customers who received a duplicate refund were not asked to return it. The duplicated amounts were reversed at the payment-processor level where the transaction had not yet settled, which covered 412 of the
640 cases. For the remaining 228, the amount was written off rather than pursued, on cost and proportionality grounds.

Cause

Evidence [EV-0f4ffcc380a8] | Account Overview S003-ACC-001 | Pages 3
GreenCart requested a Silver to Gold upgrade together with weekly settlement before its integration readiness milestones were met. Standard onboarding policy did not permit those terms at that readiness level. A conditional upgrade was approved on 20 January 2026 with phased milestones and a INR 3,00,000
security deposit, with settlement frequency moving to weekly only after milestone two is validated.
5.2 Scenario SC-005 - Shipping Label Failover (June 2026)
The primary courier provider degraded and automatic failover to the backup provider did not activate because the stored backup credentials had expired. 2,100 orders were stuck in label-pending state and 640
perishable orders breached delivery SLA. Credentials were rotated, failover was executed manually and a credential-expiry monitor was added.
5.3 Scenario SC-007 - Duplicate Refunds (September 2026)
The refund webhook consumer processed at-least-once deliveries without an idempotency check, so a broker redelivery applied 640 refunds twice, an excess of INR 1,18,000. An idempotency store was added and duplicates were reversed. Given GreenCart's cash position, the recovery was sequenced to avoid a single large debit.
6. Support Profile
GreenCart raises few tickets, typically 5 to 9 per quarter, but severity skews high because perishable delivery failures cannot be retried. Ananya Rao usually contacts support directly rather than through a ticket portal, so Support records the call and raises the ticket on her behalf.
 Fulfilment, labels and dispatch: approximately 50 percent of volume.
 Refunds and payments: approximately 30 percent.
 Connector and catalogue behaviour: approximately 20 percent.
7. Current Watch Items
1. Milestone two validation. Weekly settlement is blocked until the integration readiness milestone is signed off by Operations.
2. Failover assurance. The credential-expiry monitor added after SC-005
must be confirmed as covering both courier providers.
3. Refund reconciliation. Recovery of the SC-007 excess is being staged across settlement cycles and needs monthly confirmation.

2. Business Profile
GreenCart is the youngest account in the portfolio and the only one whose core product is perishable. Its business is built on recurring weekly subscription baskets rather than discrete purchases, which changes almost every operational assumption that applies to the other three sellers.
Subscription orders arrive in predictable batches tied to delivery slots. A delay that would be a minor inconvenience for a decor or footwear order is a total loss for fresh produce: if a same-day slot is missed, the goods are written off rather than re-delivered. GreenCart therefore treats fulfilment SLA as its primary metric and reacts to label or dispatch failures far more sharply than the other sellers.
The company is also small and capital-constrained. Cash-flow timing matters, which is why the January 2026
request for weekly settlement arrived before the account was technically ready for it, and why that request had to be handled as a documented policy exception rather than a routine change.

This project removes the interim manual processes agreed during onboarding (decision OB-001) and moves
Aurelia onto the real-time Seller API v2 integration before the festive peak.
2. Problem Statement
Aurelia went live in February 2023 on a CSV listing flow with a manual stock file uploaded twice daily. Six months of operation exposed three concrete problems.
First, the stock file cadence means published availability can be up to twelve hours stale. During normal trading this is tolerable. During a promotional window it produces oversells, and Aurelia's long manufacturing lead times make an oversell expensive to unwind.
Second, order notification by portal download and email requires a human in the loop at the seller's end.
Dispatch SLA performance degrades on weekends and public holidays for no technical reason.
Third, settlement statements retrieved manually cannot be reconciled automatically inside Aurelia's finance system, so every cycle requires manual matching. Aurelia's finance team has asked repeatedly for a machine-readable settlement feed.

This project removes the interim manual processes agreed during onboarding (decision OB-001) and moves
Aurelia onto the real-time Seller API v2 integration before the festive peak.
2. Problem Statement
Aurelia went live in February 2023 on a CSV listing flow with a manual stock file uploaded twice daily. Six months of operation exposed three concrete problems.
First, the stock file cadence means published availability can be up to twelve hours stale. During normal trading this is tolerable. During a promotional window it produces oversells, and Aurelia's long manufacturing lead times make an oversell expensive to unwind.
Second, order notification by portal download and email requires a human in the loop at the seller's end.
Dispatch SLA performance degrades on weekends and public holidays for no technical reason.
Third, settlement statements retrieved manually cannot be reconciled automatically inside Aurelia's finance system, so every cycle requires manual matching. Aurelia's finance team has asked repeatedly for a machine-readable settlement feed.

3.1 WS-1 Ledger Invariant Checks
A set of invariants now runs against every settlement batch before payout is authorised. The checks confirm that each reversal entry maps to exactly one originating order line, that the sum of entry types reconciles to the batch net, and that no entry appears more than once under its composite key.
The invariant that would have caught SC-001 is the third one. It was back-tested against twelve months of historical batches and found two further low-value anomalies from 2025, both since corrected.
3.2 WS-2 Automated Variance Detection
Each cycle is compared against a predicted payout derived from order and return events. Any seller whose variance exceeds 0.75 percent, or INR 50,000 in absolute terms, raises an operations alert before payout rather than after.
Since go-live on 10 July 2026 the control has raised four alerts across all sellers. Three were legitimate commercial adjustments. One, on 14 August 2026, was a genuine mapping error on a different account and was corrected before payout.
3.3 WS-3 Reprocessing Safety Controls
The trigger condition in SC-001 was a reprocessing run after a transient job failure. Reprocessing is now idempotent by construction: a batch carries a processing token, and a second run with the same token is rejected unless an operator explicitly authorises a replay with a documented reason.
3.4 WS-4 Seller-Facing Variance Statement
The intent is to give sellers a per-cycle statement showing predicted versus actual payout with an explanation of each difference, so that a seller's own finance team can reconcile without raising a ticket.
This workstream is three weeks behind. The delay is a dependency: the statement needs the settlement report endpoint to expose adjustment reason codes, and that change was deprioritised behind the July order
API remediation. Revised target is 16 October 2026.
3.5 WS-5 Reconciliation Runbook Update
The Payment Recovery Runbook (OPS-RB-004) is being updated to reflect the new controls, specifically the authorised-replay path introduced by WS-3 and the alert handling introduced by WS-2. Draft is with
Operations for review.

API remediation. Revised target is 16 October 2026.

5.1 Scenario SC-004 - Tax Invoice Mismatch (February 2026)
After an HSN revision, newly listed decorative lighting SKUs were not mapped to the 12 percent slab and defaulted to 18 percent. 1,240 invoices were issued at the wrong rate, producing a reconciliation mismatch of
INR 2,17,600. The mapping was corrected, credit notes were re-issued and a validation check was added to the listing workflow. The commercial decision and its rationale are recorded in the account decision record.
5.2 Scenario SC-001 - Settlement Shortfall (March 2026)
The settlement batch covering 5 to 9 March 2026 was short by INR 4,82,000. Engineering traced this to a deduplication key defect in the settlement ledger introduced during a schema migration, which double-deducted 1,914 reversal entries. The shortfall was credited on 14 March 2026. This is the highest-severity financial event on the account and remains the reference case for the reconciliation hardening project.
5.3 Scenario SC-010 - Checkout Regression (August 2026)
A platform-wide checkout release defect caused roughly 7 percent of cart-to-payment transitions to fail.
Aurelia was not the cause and was one of several affected sellers, but its festive pre-season traffic made the impact visible on the account. The release was rolled back within 34 minutes.
6. Support Profile
Aurelia raises a moderate number of tickets, typically 8 to 14 per quarter, and the distribution is unusual:
financial queries outnumber technical ones. Ritika Bansal raises tickets with precise order-level evidence attached, which shortens triage considerably. Rahul Sharma is the named support owner and handles the majority of the account's escalations.
 Settlement and payout queries: approximately 45 percent of ticket volume.
 Invoicing and tax queries: approximately 20 percent.
 Order and checkout failures: approximately 20 percent.
 Catalogue and listing questions: approximately 15 percent.
7. Current Watch Items
1. Settlement reconciliation hardening. The project opened after SC-001
is still in progress; automated variance detection is live but the seller-facing variance statement is pending.
2. Festive readiness. The account team must confirm inventory buffers and support cover before the late-September peak.
3. Tax mapping validation. The control added after SC-004 should be verified once the next HSN revision is published.

The trade-off is that production lead times are long: a stock-out on a handwoven product line can take six to eight weeks to recover, so Aurelia manages inventory conservatively and reacts strongly to any platform issue that causes phantom stock or cancelled orders.
Revenue is heavily seasonal. Roughly 38 percent of annual gross merchandise value is transacted between late September and early January, around the festive and wedding seasons. A second, smaller peak occurs in March. The account team plans catalogue campaigns, inventory buffers and support readiness around these two windows.
Aurelia's commercial sensitivity is concentrated in two areas: settlement accuracy and tax correctness.
The finance team at Aurelia reconciles every payout line against its own order export and raises a query whenever the variance exceeds one percent. This is why two of the three scenarios recorded against this account in 2026 are financial rather than technical in origin.

The primary courier provider degraded and automatic failover to the backup provider did not activate because the stored backup credentials had expired. 2,100 orders were stuck in label-pending state and 640
perishable orders breached delivery SLA. Credentials were rotated, failover was executed manually and a credential-expiry monitor was added.
5.3 Scenario SC-007 - Duplicate Refunds (September 2026)
The refund webhook consumer processed at-least-once deliveries without an idempotency check, so a broker redelivery applied 640 refunds twice, an excess of INR 1,18,000. An idempotency store was added and duplicates were reversed. Given GreenCart's cash position, the recovery was sequenced to avoid a single large debit.

 Fulfilment, labels and dispatch: approximately 50 percent of volume.
 Refunds and payments: approximately 30 percent.
 Connector and catalogue behaviour: approximately 20 percent.

1. Milestone two validation. Weekly settlement is blocked until the integration readiness milestone is signed off by Operations.
2. Failover assurance. The credential-expiry monitor added after SC-005

5.1 Scenario SC-004 - Tax Invoice Mismatch (February 2026)
After an HSN revision, newly listed decorative lighting SKUs were not mapped to the 12 percent slab and defaulted to 18 percent. 1,240 invoices were issued at the wrong rate, producing a reconciliation mismatch of
INR 2,17,600. The mapping was corrected, credit notes were re-issued and a validation check was added to the listing workflow. The commercial decision and its rationale are recorded in the account decision record.
5.2 Scenario SC-001 - Settlement Shortfall (March 2026)
The settlement batch covering 5 to 9 March 2026 was short by INR 4,82,000. Engineering traced this to a deduplication key defect in the settlement ledger introduced during a schema migration, which double-deducted 1,914 reversal entries. The shortfall was credited on 14 March 2026. This is the highest-severity financial event on the account and remains the reference case for the reconciliation hardening project.
5.3 Scenario SC-010 - Checkout Regression (August 2026)
A platform-wide checkout release defect caused roughly 7 percent of cart-to-payment transitions to fail.
Aurelia was not the cause and was one of several affected sellers, but its festive pre-season traffic made the impact visible on the account. The release was rolled back within 34 minutes.
6. Support Profile
Aurelia raises a moderate number of tickets, typically 8 to 14 per quarter, and the distribution is unusual:
financial queries outnumber technical ones. Ritika Bansal raises tickets with precise order-level evidence attached, which shortens triage considerably. Rahul Sharma is the named support owner and handles the majority of the account's escalations.
 Settlement and payout queries: approximately 45 percent of ticket volume.
 Invoicing and tax queries: approximately 20 percent.
 Order and checkout failures: approximately 20 percent.
 Catalogue and listing questions: approximately 15 percent.
7. Current Watch Items
1. Settlement reconciliation hardening. The project opened after SC-001
is still in progress; automated variance detection is live but the seller-facing variance statement is pending.
2. Festive readiness. The account team must confirm inventory buffers and support cover before the late-September peak.
3. Tax mapping validation. The control added after SC-004 should be verified once the next HSN revision is published.
Nexora Commerce Pvt. Ltd. | Nexora Marketplace

2. Business Profile
Aurelia Home Decor designs and manufactures its own range of home furnishings. Unlike a reseller, Aurelia controls its entire catalogue, which means listing quality is consistently high and attribute disputes are rare.
The trade-off is that production lead times are long: a stock-out on a handwoven product line can take six to eight weeks to recover, so Aurelia manages inventory conservatively and reacts strongly to any platform issue that causes phantom stock or cancelled orders.
Revenue is heavily seasonal. Roughly 38 percent of annual gross merchandise value is transacted between late September and early January, around the festive and wedding seasons. A second, smaller peak occurs in March. The account team plans catalogue campaigns, inventory buffers and support readiness around these two windows.
Aurelia's commercial sensitivity is concentrated in two areas: settlement accuracy and tax correctness.
The finance team at Aurelia reconciles every payout line against its own order export and raises a query whenever the variance exceeds one percent. This is why two of the three scenarios recorded against this account in 2026 are financial rather than technical in origin.

GreenCart requested a Silver to Gold upgrade together with weekly settlement before its integration readiness milestones were met. Standard onboarding policy did not permit those terms at that readiness level. A conditional upgrade was approved on 20 January 2026 with phased milestones and a INR 3,00,000
security deposit, with settlement frequency moving to weekly only after milestone two is validated.
5.2 Scenario SC-005 - Shipping Label Failover (June 2026)
The primary courier provider degraded and automatic failover to the backup provider did not activate because the stored backup credentials had expired. 2,100 orders were stuck in label-pending state and 640
perishable orders breached delivery SLA. Credentials were rotated, failover was executed manually and a credential-expiry monitor was added.
5.3 Scenario SC-007 - Duplicate Refunds (September 2026)
The refund webhook consumer processed at-least-once deliveries without an idempotency check, so a broker redelivery applied 640 refunds twice, an excess of INR 1,18,000. An idempotency store was added and duplicates were reversed. Given GreenCart's cash position, the recovery was sequenced to avoid a single large debit.
6. Support Profile
GreenCart raises few tickets, typically 5 to 9 per quarter, but severity skews high because perishable delivery failures cannot be retried. Ananya Rao usually contacts support directly rather than through a ticket portal, so Support records the call and raises the ticket on her behalf.
 Fulfilment, labels and dispatch: approximately 50 percent of volume.
 Refunds and payments: approximately 30 percent.
 Connector and catalogue behaviour: approximately 20 percent.
7. Current Watch Items
1. Milestone two validation. Weekly settlement is blocked until the integration readiness milestone is signed off by Operations.
2. Failover assurance. The credential-expiry monitor added after SC-005
must be confirmed as covering both courier providers.
3. Refund reconciliation. Recovery of the SC-007 excess is being staged across settlement cycles and needs monthly confirmation.

Engineering found that the deduplication key used by the settlement ledger no longer included the order identifier for reversal entries. The key was changed during the v1.8 to v1.9 schema migration. 5.1 Scenario SC-004 - Tax Invoice Mismatch (February 2026)
After an HSN revision, newly listed decorative lighting SKUs were not mapped to the 12 percent slab and defaulted to 18 percent. 1,240 invoices were issued at the wrong rate, producing a reconciliation mismatch of
INR 2,17,600. The mapping was corrected, credit notes were re-issued and a validation check was added to the listing workflow. The commercial decision and its rationale are recorded in the account decision record.
5.2 Scenario SC-001 - Settlement Shortfall (March 2026)
The settlement batch covering 5 to 9 March 2026 was short by INR 4,82,000. Engineering traced this to a deduplication key defect in the settlement ledger introduced during a schema migration, which double-deducted 1,914 reversal entries. The shortfall was credited on 14 March 2026. This is the highest-severity financial event on the account and remains the reference case for the reconciliation hardening project.
5.3 Scenario SC-010 - Checkout Regression (August 2026)
A platform-wide checkout release defect caused roughly 7 percent of cart-to-payment transitions to fail.
Aurelia was not the cause and was one of several affected sellers, but its festive pre-season traffic made the impact visible on the account. The release was rolled back within 34 minutes.

3. Tax mapping validation. The control added after SC-004 should be verified once the next HSN revision is published.

2. Business Profile
Aurelia Home Decor designs and manufactures its own range of home furnishings. Unlike a reseller, Aurelia controls its entire catalogue, which means listing quality is consistently high and attribute disputes are rare.
The trade-off is that production lead times are long: a stock-out on a handwoven product line can take six to eight weeks to recover, so Aurelia manages inventory conservatively and reacts strongly to any platform issue that causes phantom stock or cancelled orders.
Revenue is heavily seasonal. Roughly 38 percent of annual gross merchandise value is transacted between late September and early January, around the festive and wedding seasons. A second, smaller peak occurs in March. The account team plans catalogue campaigns, inventory buffers and support readiness around these two windows.
Aurelia's commercial sensitivity is concentrated in two areas: settlement accuracy and tax correctness.
The finance team at Aurelia reconciles every payout line against its own order export and raises a query whenever the variance exceeds one percent. This is why two of the three scenarios recorded against this account in 2026 are financial rather than technical in origin.

Escalated to Engineering at 11:20 IST on 12 March, within the P1 escalation window defined in the Seller

I also flagged the ticket to Aditya Verma at 11:25 IST, because Aurelia's finance team reconciles every cycle and a two-day payout delay on a Gold account needed an account-manager conversation rather than a support update.

Root Cause as Reported Back to Support
Engineering found that the deduplication key used by the settlement ledger no longer included the order identifier for reversal entries. The key was changed during the v1.8 to v1.9 schema migration. When the batch was reprocessed after a transient job failure, the ledger treated each reversal as a new entry rather than as an existing one, so every reversal was deducted a second time.
Full technical detail is in INC-2026-0312.
Resolution
The deduplication key was corrected to include order identifier plus entry type. The affected batch was reprocessed, Operations verified the corrected payout against the Payment Recovery Runbook
(OPS-RB-004), and INR 4,82,000 was credited on 14 March 2026. The applicable rule is the platform's accountability for the accuracy of a computed settlement under the Payment and Settlement Policy
(POL-FIN-002).

Both of those were written for order events. Nobody revisited the refund consumer against the same requirement. It had also never been restarted under load in a way that produced a meaningful redelivery volume, so the defect had no opportunity to surface.
8. Root Cause
The refund webhook consumer applied refund events without checking whether an event had already been processed. Because the event broker provides at-least-once delivery, a rolling restart during a deployment caused 640 processed-but-unacknowledged events to be redelivered and applied a second time, issuing duplicate refunds totalling INR 1,18,000 in excess.
9. Contributing Factors
1. No idempotency check on a financial operation consuming an at-least-once stream.
2. Requirement not applied consistently. At-least-once handling was required for order events and never audited across other consumers.
3. No refund volume monitoring per account against expected volume.
4. Grace period shorter than the acknowledgement path, making redelivery likely on any rolling restart.
5. Deployment performed during the account's peak refund window, evening being when quality reports are raised.
6. Duplicate refunds are silent. Each one succeeds; nothing fails.
10. Mitigation
The idempotency store was deployed at 16:30 on 4 September, which stopped any further duplication.
Before that, no mitigation was applied: the duplication had already ended at 02:40 when the redelivery backlog cleared, so there was no ongoing harm to stop.
The substantive mitigation question was financial rather than technical, and it belonged to Operations: how to recover INR 1,18,000 from a cash- constrained seller who had not caused the error.
The decision was to recover across four settlement cycles beginning 15 September, with no interest or fee.
Customers who received a duplicate refund were not asked to return it. Both the idempotency requirement and the staged recovery default are set by the Payment and Settlement Policy (POL-FIN-002) and executed under the Payment Recovery Runbook (OPS-RB-004).

8. Root Cause
The refund webhook consumer applied refund events without checking whether an event had already been processed. Because the event broker provides at-least-once delivery, a rolling restart during a deployment caused 640 processed-but-unacknowledged events to be redelivered and applied a second time, issuing duplicate refunds totalling INR 1,18,000 in excess.
9. Contributing Factors
1. No idempotency check on a financial operation consuming an at-least-once stream.
2. Requirement not applied consistently. At-least-once handling was required for order events and never audited across other consumers.
3. No refund volume monitoring per account against expected volume.
4. Grace period shorter than the acknowledgement path, making redelivery likely on any rolling restart.
5. Deployment performed during the account's peak refund window, evening being when quality reports are raised.
6. Duplicate refunds are silent. Each one succeeds; nothing fails.
10. Mitigation
The idempotency store was deployed at 16:30 on 4 September, which stopped any further duplication.
Before that, no mitigation was applied: the duplication had already ended at 02:40 when the redelivery backlog cleared, so there was no ongoing harm to stop.
The substantive mitigation question was financial rather than technical, and it belonged to Operations: how to recover INR 1,18,000 from a cash- constrained seller who had not caused the error.
The decision was to recover across four settlement cycles beginning 15 September, with no interest or fee.
Customers who received a duplicate refund were not asked to return it. Both the idempotency requirement and the staged recovery default are set by the Payment and Settlement Policy (POL-FIN-002) and executed under the Payment Recovery Runbook (OPS-RB-004).

8. Root Cause
The refund webhook consumer applied refund events without checking whether an event had already been processed. Because the event broker provides at-least-once delivery, a rolling restart during a deployment caused 640 processed-but-unacknowledged events to be redelivered and applied a second time, issuing duplicate refunds totalling INR 1,18,000 in excess.
9. Contributing Factors
1. No idempotency check on a financial operation consuming an at-least-once stream.
2. Requirement not applied consistently. At-least-once handling was required for order events and never audited across other consumers.
3. No refund volume monitoring per account against expected volume.
4. Grace period shorter than the acknowledgement path, making redelivery likely on any rolling restart.
5. Deployment performed during the account's peak refund window, evening being when quality reports are raised.
6. Duplicate refunds are silent. Each one succeeds; nothing fails.
10. Mitigation
The idempotency store was deployed at 16:30 on 4 September, which stopped any further duplication.
Before that, no mitigation was applied: the duplication had already ended at 02:40 when the redelivery backlog cleared, so there was no ongoing harm to stop.
The substantive mitigation question was financial rather than technical, and it belonged to Operations: how to recover INR 1,18,000 from a cash- constrained seller who had not caused the error.
The decision was to recover across four settlement cycles beginning 15 September, with no interest or fee.
Customers who received a duplicate refund were not asked to return it. Both the idempotency requirement and the staged recovery default are set by the Payment and Settlement Policy (POL-FIN-002) and executed under the Payment Recovery Runbook (OPS-RB-004).

The concentration on a single seller was structural rather than account-specific. GreenCart operates under a refund-on-report category exception for perishable goods: a customer reporting a quality problem is refunded without a physical return. This account therefore generates several times more refund events per order than any other seller, so a defect in refund processing surfaces here first and hardest.

Detected by the seller, approximately 20 hours after the first duplicate.

There was no platform-side control that would have detected this. Refund volume per account was not monitored against expected volume, and duplicate refund application produced no error: each individual refund succeeded.

Both of those were written for order events. Nobody revisited the refund consumer against the same requirement. It had also never been restarted under load in a way that produced a meaningful redelivery volume, so the defect had no opportunity to surface.
8. Root Cause
The refund webhook consumer applied refund events without checking whether an event had already been processed. Because the event broker provides at-least-once delivery, a rolling restart during a deployment caused 640 processed-but-unacknowledged events to be redelivered and applied a second time, issuing duplicate refunds totalling INR 1,18,000 in excess.
9. Contributing Factors
1. No idempotency check on a financial operation consuming an at-least-once stream.
2. Requirement not applied consistently. At-least-once handling was required for order events and never audited across other consumers.
3. No refund volume monitoring per account against expected volume.
4. Grace period shorter than the acknowledgement path, making redelivery likely on any rolling restart.
5. Deployment performed during the account's peak refund window, evening being when quality reports are raised.
6. Duplicate refunds are silent. Each one succeeds; nothing fails.
10. Mitigation
The idempotency store was deployed at 16:30 on 4 September, which stopped any further duplication.
Before that, no mitigation was applied: the duplication had already ended at 02:40 when the redelivery backlog cleared, so there was no ongoing harm to stop.
The substantive mitigation question was financial rather than technical, and it belonged to Operations: how to recover INR 1,18,000 from a cash- constrained seller who had not caused the error.
The decision was to recover across four settlement cycles beginning 15 September, with no interest or fee.
Customers who received a duplicate refund were not asked to return it. Both the idempotency requirement and the staged recovery default are set by the Payment and Settlement Policy (POL-FIN-002) and executed under the Payment Recovery Runbook (OPS-RB-004).
